figures.name: model_progression
figures.caption: Typed entity F1 and character-level error rates for TinyBERT INT8 and DeBERTa INT8 on the same held-out validation split.

figures.name: deberta_fp32_vs_int8
figures.caption: FP32 and INT8 typed entity F1 on every evaluation view, with the F1 lost to quantization against the 0.02 release gate.

figures.name: deberta_split_performance
figures.caption: Typed entity precision/recall/F1 and private-character recall for the deployed INT8 model on each evaluation view.

figures.name: per_entity_f1
figures.caption: Typed entity F1 per entity type on the combined validation view, annotated with gold support.

figures.name: ood_model_comparison
figures.caption: TinyBERT INT8 against DeBERTa INT8 on the OOD development and frozen final fixtures, model-only in both cases.

figures.name: model_size_comparison
figures.caption: On-disk size of every privacy-model artifact, deployed one highlighted.

figures.name: latency_by_input_length
figures.caption: Median single-threaded inference latency against input length for all three deployment candidates, on the development workstation.

figures.name: cpu_latency_distribution
figures.caption: Per-row masking latency distribution and cumulative distribution for the current system on the workstation and on a Raspberry Pi 5.

figures.name: pipeline_latency_breakdown
figures.caption: Mean latency of each stage inside a masking call and across the assembled pipeline, for the current system on the Raspberry Pi 5. The two audio stages are driven by a synthesised probe tone rather than speech; the real-speech cost is in the audio benchmark section.

figures.name: cpu_memory_and_throughput
figures.caption: Peak process RSS, resident privacy-stack cost and masking throughput for the current system on the workstation and on a Raspberry Pi 5.

figures.name: deployment_parity
figures.caption: Cross-device agreement and quality difference for the current system running the identical INT8 artifact on the workstation and a Raspberry Pi 5. Disagreement is INT8 kernel arithmetic differing between x86-64 and aarch64, not a different model.

figures.name: audio_pipeline_stage_latency
figures.caption: Mean per-clip latency of every pipeline stage from audio to post-mask text, and each stage's share of total processing time, for the current system on the Raspberry Pi 5.

figures.name: audio_duration_scaling
figures.caption: Audio duration against end-to-end latency, STT latency and STT real-time factor for the current system on the Raspberry Pi 5. RTF below 1 means the device processes speech faster than it arrives; points above the dashed line are clips it did not.

figures.name: audio_latency_by_duration_bucket
figures.caption: Mean end-to-end latency per clip-duration bucket for the current system on the Raspberry Pi 5, with the observed minimum and maximum as whiskers.

figures.name: audio_latency_and_memory
figures.caption: Cumulative distribution of end-to-end latency with P50/P90/P95/P99, and resident memory as each model loads, for the current system on the Raspberry Pi 5, against the 4 GB Raspberry Pi budget.

figures.name: audio_privacy_reference_vs_pipeline
figures.caption: Private-character recall and leakage for the same clips scored from written reference text, from uncased unpunctuated reference text, and end to end from audio; plus the attribution of every end-to-end failure. Current system on the Raspberry Pi 5.

figures.name: audio_word_error_rate
figures.caption: Word error rate on the synthetic privacy clips and on the LibriSpeech dev-clean clips, reported separately because they are different distributions. Current system on the Raspberry Pi 5.

figures.name: audio_postprocessing_amplification
figures.caption: The spoken-digit finding: utterances where the privacy model did not mask a spoken number and the display renderer then rendered it as a numeral. Shown for every recognizer generation, because the Whisper-era count is zero by change of orthography rather than by a change to the renderer.

figures.name: stt_engine_accuracy
figures.caption: Word error rate and number handling for every measured recognizer on the committed audio benchmark. The raw word error rate is shown in grey to expose how much of it is spelling: Canary wrote numbers as words, Whisper writes numerals, and only the number-normalised bars compare the engines. The right panel separates transcribing a long number correctly from keeping it out of the released text - the two are not the same thing, and the engines differ in opposite directions.

figures.name: stt_engine_cost
figures.caption: Real-time factor and end-to-end latency for every measured recognizer. The dashed line is real time: a bar below it means the device processes speech faster than it arrives. Bars are drawn only for arms that have been measured.

figures.name: stt_engine_released_identifiers
figures.caption: End-to-end privacy per recognizer. Left: the measure that survives a change of recognizer without any alignment - after masking and after the display renderer, is an identifier-scale number still legible in what the device released? Right: the share of annotated entities that reached no released text, recomputed for every arm by privacy_eval.rescore so that one scoring definition is applied throughout.

figures.name: current_system_device_cost
figures.caption: Real-time factor, end-to-end latency and peak memory for the current system on the workstation and on a Raspberry Pi 5. RTF below the dashed line means the device processes speech faster than it arrives; the black rule on each bar is the P90. On the Raspberry Pi the P90 sits above the line, and the clips responsible are the shortest ones - Whisper decodes a fixed window whatever the clip length, so the per-clip cost has a floor.

figures.name: current_system_device_quality
figures.caption: Recognition accuracy, end-to-end privacy after speech recognition, and privacy-model quality on text, for the current system on both devices. Every pair is measured on the same committed fixtures through the same INT8 artifact; the residual differences are INT8 kernel arithmetic on aarch64 against x86-64.

figures.name: assistant_privacy_boundary
figures.caption: What reached the outbound request, what the local pipeline cost, and the local guarantees, for the current system on both devices. The boundary counts are read off the bytes handed to urllib. The Raspberry Pi run had no API key, so its requests were built and audited but never sent; the network, placeholder-preservation and TTS measurements are workstation only and are reported as such.

The privacy columns are recomputed for every run on the current scoring definition by privacy_eval.rescore, so a folder written before the alignment fix is not compared against one written after it. `aggregate_wer` is each run's own raw figure and is not comparable between recognizers; `aggregate_wer_number_normalised` is.

tables.name: stt_engine_comparison
tables.caption: Every measured recognizer arm, scored from its saved transcripts by one implementation. Arms that were never measured on a device are absent rather than zero. `drawn_in_figures` marks the arms the charts show; the previous system's Whisper rows are provenance for the current ones.

tables.name: stt_engine_privacy
tables.caption: End-to-end privacy per recognizer arm. The entity- and character-level columns are recomputed for every arm by privacy_eval.rescore on one definition - spoken numbers folded on both sides, located regions trimmed to their alphanumeric core - so they are comparable across engines; the released-identifier columns need no alignment at all.

tables.name: current_system_inherits_previous_core

tables.name: assistant_privacy_boundary
tables.caption: The assistant round trip on each device: what reached the outbound request, what the local legs cost, and which live-only measurements exist. Blank or zero live columns on the Raspberry Pi row mean the leg was not attempted because no API key was configured, not that it failed.
